title: US Treasury Secretary Bessent Warns Fed Hike Amid Growing AI Bubble Concerns
body:
Traders have sharply trimmed their bets on a dramatic Federal Reserve rate hike after a wave of tech earnings and the record‑breaking debut of AI‑focused firm Anthropic failed to spark broader market optimism. The shift comes as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent cautioned that the central bank could “overtighten” and jeopardize the fragile recovery, underscoring growing unease about the sustainability of the current AI‑driven rally.

The market’s recalibration was evident on Monday’s futures trading, where the probability of a 0.5‑percentage‑point increase at the December 9 policy meeting fell from roughly 70 percent late last week to just under 40 percent. The downgrade reflects a broader reassessment of inflationary pressures after the tech sector’s earnings season delivered mixed signals. While giants such as Microsoft and Alphabet posted solid top‑line growth, they also flagged higher spending on AI infrastructure and warned that talent shortages could temper profit margins. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s $4.1 billion initial public offering— the largest for an AI‑centric company since the 2021 boom—raised concerns that valuations are inflating faster than the underlying revenue base can support.

Bessent’s remarks, delivered at a press conference in Washington, highlighted the delicate balance policymakers must strike. “If the Fed pushes too hard, too fast, we risk choking off the very momentum that is beginning to lift the economy out of recessionary headwinds,” he said. The Treasury secretary’s warning aligns with a growing chorus of economists who argue that the Fed’s aggressive tightening cycle—nine rate hikes since March 2022—has already squeezed credit and could dampen consumer spending if continued at the same pace. The warning carries particular weight because Bessent, a former chief economist at BlackRock, is widely regarded as an influential voice on monetary policy.

Investors are now parsing the implications of a potentially more dovish Fed stance. A milder rate hike, or even a pause, would likely buoy risk assets and keep the dollar from appreciating further—a scenario that could benefit U.S. exporters and emerging‑market economies still grappling with high borrowing costs. Conversely, if the Fed decides that inflation remains too sticky, it may still opt for a half‑point increase, a move that would shock markets already jittery from the recent correction. The uncertainty is reflected in the widening spread between the 2‑year Treasury yield and the 10‑year benchmark, a traditional barometer of investor confidence in the Fed’s trajectory.

Analysts also point to the “AI bubble” narrative gaining traction among skeptics. While AI promises transformative productivity gains, the sector’s capital influx has been rapid, with venture capital pouring billions into startups that have yet to prove commercial viability. The Anthropic IPO, which priced at a 60‑percent premium to its private valuation, has intensified debate over whether the market is pricing in unrealistic growth assumptions. Some equity strategists warn that a correction in AI‑related stocks could spill over into broader technology indices, amplifying volatility and prompting the Fed to err on the side of caution.

Looking ahead, the December policy meeting will serve as a litmus test for the Fed’s assessment of inflation trends, labor market resilience, and the impact of AI‑driven investment on the economy. Market participants will be watching upcoming data releases—particularly the consumer price index and jobless claims—to gauge whether the central bank can afford a more measured approach. If the Fed signals a pause or a smaller hike, it could restore confidence in the equity markets and sustain the current, albeit cautious, optimism around AI. However, a decisive move to raise rates sharply could reignite concerns about overtightening, potentially triggering another bout of market turbulence. The coming weeks will thus determine whether the economy can ride the AI wave without being derailed by monetary policy missteps.
